implementation_notes: Core Animation provides the timer: CADisplayLink is 'a timer object that allows your app to synchronize its drawing to the refresh rate of the display'; you add it to a run loop and 'the system calls the selector on the target when the screen's contents need to update', with timestamp giving 'the time the system displayed the previous frame' and targetTimestamp 'when the next frame displays'. What replaces the classic structure: the run loop owns the cadence and calls back per display refresh - compute dt from timestamp deltas, accumulate a fixed step and render inside the callback. The frame rate is only a preference: preferredFramesPerSecond is rounded to a divisor of the display's maximum refresh rate (a 60 Hz device allows 15, 20, 30 or 60), and the actual rate can drop under Low Power Mode or thermal pressure.
pitfalls: CADisplayLink retains its target, so a controller that owns the link and is also its target creates a retain cycle - hold the link weakly or invalidate() it on teardown.
Add the link in .common run-loop mode when the UI scrolls or tracks; in the default mode it pauses during scrolling and the simulation silently freezes.
preferredFramesPerSecond is a preference only: the system rounds it to a divisor of the maximum refresh rate and may reduce it for power or thermal reasons, so real dt varies - never assume 60 Hz.
The callback runs on the main run loop: blocking or heavy work in step drops frames and delays input; use the display link for presentation cadence, not for compute.

variants.name: SpriteKit SKScene frame-cycle callbacks
variants.implementation_notes: SpriteKit owns the whole loop: to display a scene you present it from an SKView, and the framework calls the scene's frame-cycle callbacks - update(_:) 'tells your app to perform any app-specific logic to update your scene' every frame, followed in documented order by didEvaluateActions(), didSimulatePhysics() and didApplyConstraints(), with SKSceneDelegate offering the same hooks without subclassing. What replaces the classic structure: the engine's animation loop replaces the driver and its physics stage replaces the fixed-step integration - implement update for game logic, put physics-dependent work after didSimulatePhysics, and let the view own frame pacing. Choose it when the game is scene-graph shaped; choose CADisplayLink when you render yourself and need the raw frame callback.
pitfalls: update(_:) runs before actions and physics, so reading post-simulation positions there gives stale data - use didSimulatePhysics for that.
SpriteKit has no fixed-step API and frame time varies with the display and device; a deterministic simulation needs its own fixed-step accumulator inside update.
The scene's frame cycle stops when the view is paused or the app is backgrounded; do not rely on it as a wall-clock timer for simulation that must keep advancing.
All callbacks run on the main thread: heavy work moves to background queues and hands results back.
